notes: DETAILED PTERIDOPHYTE (Dryopteris) MORPHOLOGY AND REPRODUCTION.
Rhizome: short, creeping, bearing scales + adventitious roots; the main vegetative organ.
Frond: the leaf-like organ; stipe (stalk) + blade (lamina); blade divided into pinnae, each into pinules.
Sori: clusters of sporangia on the underside of the pinnae; often covered by an indusium (a flap of tissue).
Sporangium: bears an annulus (a row of specialized cells for dehiscence); meiosis in the spore mother cell → spores (n).
Spore: one-celled, motile-free, wind-dispersed; germinates in moist conditions.
Prothallus (gametophyte): small, heart-shaped, free-living; bears antheridia (male) + archegonia (female); produces biflagellated sperm + egg.
Fertilisation: sperm swims through water to the egg → zygote (2n) → young sporophyte (dependent on the prothallus initially).
Young sporophyte: develops a rhizome + fronds; becomes independent; the prothallus withers.
Life cycle: alternation of generations with SPOROPHYTE (2n) dominant; gametophyte (n) small, free-living, and short-lived.
Key difference from bryophytes: true vascular tissue (xylem + phloem) + dominant sporophyte.
Economic importance: medicinal (ferns in traditional medicine), ornamental (garden ferns), soil stabilisation; fossil pteridophytes form coal deposits.
Other pteridophytes: horsetails (Equisetum — jointed, silica), clubmosses (Lycopodium — cones), tree ferns (Cyathea).
NEB focus: detailed Dryopteris frond + rhizome structure, sori/annulus, the prothallus, and the full life cycle.
confusion: The prothallus (gametophyte) is small and heart-shaped; it is NOT the main plant body (that is the frond-bearing sporophyte).
Sori are clusters of sporangia on the frond underside; the indusium covers them (not the sori themselves).
The annulus is the specialized dehiscent structure of the sporangium (a row of cells that snaps the capsule open).
Fertilisation STILL requires water in pteridophytes (flagellated sperm) — a key exam point.
The young sporophyte is initially dependent on the prothallus; it becomes independent as it develops its own rhizome + fronds.
Pteridophytes have TRUE vascular tissue; bryophytes do NOT — the key distinction.

enrichedContent.summary: A detailed study of Dryopteris (fern) shows a short, creeping, scaled rhizome bearing adventitious roots and fronds. The frond (stipe + blade) has pinnae and pinules, with sori (clusters of sporangia with an annulus and indusium) on the underside. Meiosis in the spore mother cell produces spores that germinate into the small, heart-shaped prothallus (gametophyte), which bears antheridia and archegonia. Fertilisation requires water; the zygote develops into the dominant sporophyte. Pteridophytes are distinguished from bryophytes by their true vascular tissue and dominant sporophyte. NEB focuses on the detailed frond + rhizome structure, sori/annulus, prothallus, and the full life cycle.

summary: A detailed study of Dryopteris (fern) shows a short, creeping, scaled rhizome bearing adventitious roots and fronds. The frond (stipe + blade) has pinnae and pinules, with sori (clusters of sporangia with an annulus and indusium) on the underside. Meiosis in the spore mother cell produces spores that germinate into the small, heart-shaped prothallus (gametophyte), which bears antheridia and archegonia. Fertilisation requires water; the zygote develops into the dominant sporophyte. Pteridophytes are distinguished from bryophytes by their true vascular tissue and dominant sporophyte. NEB focuses on the detailed frond + rhizome structure, sori/annulus, prothallus, and the full life cycle. Pteridophytes are seedless vascular plants that represent the evolutionary transition between non-vascular bryophytes and seed-bearing plants. The sporophyte (2n) is the dominant generation; the gametophyte (prothallus) is small and free-living. Ferns like Dryopteris have fronds with sori (spore clusters). Fertilisation still requires water. Pteridophytes are economically important as medicinal herbs, ornamentals, soil stabilisers, and the source of coal deposits.
